props.title: Let's Make Love

sections.content: Let's Make Love (1960) represents one of Marilyn Monroe's final completed films, coming just two years before her death. The musical comedy showcases Monroe at the height of her star power, though it's often overshadowed by her more iconic works like Some Like It Hot (1959) and The Seven Year Itch (1955). The production was notably troubled - original director Gregory Ratoff died during pre-production, and the script went through multiple rewrites. Yet it provides fascinating insight into both Hollywood's dying studio system and Monroe's evolving screen persona.

sections.content: The film's plot - about a billionaire who goes undercover in an off-Broadway show to woo an actress - feels like a throwback to 1930s screwball comedies like Easy Living (1937) and My Man Godfrey (1936). But director George Cukor, known for classics like The Philadelphia Story (1940), brings a modern sensibility. The musical numbers, while not groundbreaking, capture the transition period between classic Hollywood musicals and the more realistic style that would emerge in films like West Side Story (1961).

Yves Montand's performance as the billionaire Jean-Marc Clement marked a rare Hollywood appearance for the French star. His chemistry with Monroe echoes their real-life affair during filming, adding an extra layer of complexity to their scenes together. The supporting cast includes comedy legends Milton Berle and Tony Randall, whose presence bridges the vaudeville era with modern comedy styles emerging in films like Pillow Talk (1959). sections.content: Let's Make Love arrived at a crucial turning point in Hollywood history. The studio system was crumbling, television was stealing audiences, and new European cinema was challenging American dominance. Monroe's performance style - a mix of comedy and vulnerability that influenced later actresses like Michelle Williams in My Week with Marilyn (2011) - represents the last gasp of classical Hollywood star power before the industry's radical transformation in the 1960s.
